summary: Defines how a Mobile IPv6 node can bootstrap a Home Agent address, home address, and IPsec associations from pre-configured credentials, instead of static setup. It addresses the split scenario from RFC 4640. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: Mobile IPv6 needs a device to know its Home Agent, home address, and security settings. RFC 5026 explains how the device and service can obtain or configure these details during a secure setup.

questions: how does mipv6 find a home agent
how does mobile ipv6 find a home agent

subtitle: How a Mobile IPv6 node can find a Home Agent and configure its security and home address.

tldr.problem: A Mobile IPv6 node needs a Home Agent address, a home address, and IPsec security associations. Manually configuring every node can become difficult as their number grows.
tldr.mechanism: The node uses a preconfigured provider domain name to find a Home Agent through DNS, establishes IPsec with IKEv2, and obtains or configures a home address. The Home Agent can also update DNS for that address.
tldr.outcome: The procedures address the split scenario, where network access and mobility service are authorized by different parties. RFC 5026 is updated by RFC 8553.

today: RFC 5026 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2007 and is updated by RFC 8553.

sections.title: The Bootstrapping Problem
sections.content:
A Mobile IPv6 node needs the address of its Home Agent, a home address, and cryptographic material for IPsec security associations before it can use the service. The base Mobile IPv6 specification does not define how to acquire all of these automatically, so administrators may need to configure them manually.

RFC 5026 describes bootstrapping when the party authorizing network access differs from the party authorizing mobility service. Its solution is also applicable to other bootstrapping cases described as more specific forms of this split scenario.
sections.plainLanguage: A Mobile IPv6 device needs a Home Agent, a home address, and security settings before it can connect. This RFC describes how to obtain these details instead of configuring each one entirely by hand.

sections.title: The Split Scenario
sections.content:
The Access Service Authorizer (ASA) approves a node for network access. The Mobility Service Authorizer (MSA) approves the node for Mobile IPv6 service. In the split scenario, these are different entities. The RFC gives the example of an enterprise Home Agent used while the user reaches the Internet through a separate access provider.

The Mobility Service Provider (MSP) operates the mobility service and may or may not be the same organization as the MSA. The Home Agent may authenticate the node using certificates or EAP through an AAA system. The backend communication between the Home Agent and AAA system is outside the RFC's scope.
sections.plainLanguage: The organization that provides Internet access can differ from the organization that approves mobility service. The RFC explains how the mobile node and Home Agent handle that separation.

sections.title: The Main Bootstrapping Steps
sections.content:
The node discovers a Home Agent using DNS. A configured provider domain name is enough for the service-name lookup, which uses a DNS SRV record. The node then uses IKEv2 to establish IPsec security associations and obtains a home address from the Home Agent or configures one itself.

The Home Agent may need to contact the MSA to authenticate the user and authorize mobility service. An optional part of the process lets the node request that its fully qualified domain name be updated with its current home address.
sections.plainLanguage: The node finds a Home Agent, establishes security with it, and gets a home address. The Home Agent may also check authorization and update the node's DNS record.

sections.title: Finding a Home Agent with DNS
sections.content:
The node can look up a configured Home Agent name with an AAAA query. Alternatively, it can look up a service using the name _mip6._ipv6 and an SRV record. The service name is mip6, and the protocol name is ipv6.

An SRV answer can list multiple Home Agents with preference and weight values. If the chosen Home Agent does not respond to IKE_SA_INIT or IKEv2 authentication fails, the node SHOULD try another listed Home Agent. The RFC does not define a specific load-balancing mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The node asks DNS for a Home Agent address or a list of Home Agent services. If one listed Home Agent fails to respond or authenticate, the node can try another.

sections.title: Assigning and Registering a Home Address
sections.content:
During IKEv2, the node can ask the Home Agent to assign a home address. It may instead request a home prefix and configure its own address. If the Home Agent does not permit auto-configuration, it returns an assigned address that the node must use. If duplicate address detection fails, the node selects another address and establishes new child security associations.

When a dynamic address changes, an existing DNS record may no longer be valid. The node can include a DNS Update mobility option in a Binding Update, asking the Home Agent to create or remove the record. The Home Agent must authorize the requested name before updating it; RFC 5026 is updated by RFC 8553.
sections.plainLanguage: The Home Agent can assign an address, or provide a prefix for the node to configure one. A DNS update can keep the node's name linked to its current address.

messages.label: IKEv2 exchange
messages.note: Establishes IPsec and configures the home address.

messages.label: Binding Update
messages.note: Can include a DNS Update option with the node's name.
